topic: The Role of Markets and Money
subject: economics

moments.title: A Monetary History of the United States
moments.body: Friedman and Schwartz argue from US data that the Great Depression was made far worse by the Federal Reserve's failure to prevent monetary contraction. The book reframes monetary policy as crucial — a direct challenge to the Keynesian consensus.
moments.takeaway: Re-analysis of historical data can challenge a prevailing macroeconomic interpretation.

moments.title: The Role of Monetary Policy
moments.body: Friedman argues there is no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment — the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the 'natural rate' of unemployment. Edmund Phelps had reached similar conclusions independently. The 1970s stagflation provides empirical support.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical prediction precedes its empirical confirmation by years; both then reshape policy.

moments.title: Volcker's disinflation
moments.body: Volcker, appointed Fed chair in 1979, raises interest rates dramatically (Fed Funds rate peaks at 19% in 1981) to break inflation. US unemployment peaks at 10.8% in 1982. Inflation falls from 13.5% in 1980 to 3.2% by 1983. The disinflation is painful but lasting.
moments.takeaway: Severe monetary tightening can break inflation — at substantial short-run cost. The Volcker disinflation reshaped central bank credibility.

now.title: After monetarism
now.body: Strict monetarism (control of monetary aggregates) was abandoned by most central banks in the 1990s as money-velocity relationships became unstable. Inflation targeting (NZ 1989, UK 1992, Sweden 1993) became the new orthodoxy. Friedman's broader insight — that monetary policy matters and central bank credibility is foundational — remains influential.
now.open_questions: How should central banks operate in a world of repeatedly hitting the zero lower bound? The post-2008 toolkit (QE, forward guidance) is partly an answer.

reflection: Friedman did to mid-century Keynesianism what Keynes had done to pre-1936 orthodoxy. The intellectual cycle continued after 2008 with the partial Keynesian revival.
